questions: Are your hands shaking or moving in a way that feels out of your control?
Does this happen when you are resting, moving, or both?
Do these movements stop when you focus on doing something else with your hands?
Have you experienced any weakness or numbness in your arms or hands?
Have you had any recent head injury or illness?
Do you have a family history of similar movements?
Do you feel anxious or stressed when these movements occur?
Have you tried any medications for this?
Do the movements affect your ability to perform daily tasks?
Have you noticed these movements getting worse over time?

results: 1. Detailed bedside neurological examination focusing on functional tremor signs
distractibility testing (complex motor task with the unaffected side): POSITIVE - the tremor decreases or stops when the left arm performs a task such as drinking from a cup
co-activation sign on passive movement of the affected limb: POSITIVE - movement of the contralateral arm co-activates the hand with an increase in tremor intensity
'whack-a-mole' sign (restrain the affected limb and watch the others): POSITIVE - passive fixation of the hand increases movement in the arm and shoulder
anticipatory jerk to a feigned tendon-hammer approach (Hallett sign): absent
suggestibility / sham stimulus (tuning fork or vibration applied as 'treatment'): no change
variability of amplitude, frequency and axis over the examination: irregular, variable frequency around 4-6 Hz, at times combined with myoclonic jerks
2. Tremor entrainment test (asking patient to tap with the non-affected hand at different frequencies)
entrainment testing (tap to an externally paced rhythm): POSITIVE - amplitude falls and the rhythm becomes irregular under repetitive voluntary movement of the other side
3. Arm raise test (holding arms outstretched and observing for tremor changes)
not performed / not available
4. Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) assessment
posture and pull test: normal
muscle tone (spasticity, rigidity, paratonia): normal
finger-tapping for bradykinesia and decrement: no decrement - argues against Parkinson disease
cognitive screen: normal

full blood count, renal and liver profile: normal

TSH / free T4: normal
